## Unit 4A Comparing mortgage programs

Proposed future OIL allocation, 50 minutes: instruction and worked example 25; applied practice 10; peer and instructor dialogue with revision 10; formative checks and feedback 5. Allocation includes active work and must be tested with learners.

### A program name is the start of a comparison

A mortgage program describes a financing channel and its requirements. It does not describe every feature of an individual loan. Two loans in the same program can have different rates, costs, permissible structures, and lender requirements. A borrower who asks for the lowest payment may actually need a manageable total housing expense, enough remaining savings, and protection from a payment increase. Those concerns require more than a label.

Begin by recording the purpose, property, expected occupancy, available funds, income documentation, existing obligations, and the borrower's plans. Then investigate plausible options using current sources. Eligibility information supports that investigation; it is not a substitute for an application, verification, or underwriting. A program can be available in principle while the proposed borrower, property, or transaction fails a particular requirement.

Do not import a colleague's remembered minimum credit score, maximum debt ratio, annual fee, or county limit into the discussion as a universal rule. Identify whether a requirement comes from law, a government program, an investor, or a lender. Record the version and relevant effective date. A lender may impose additional requirements within applicable law; an institutional requirement should not be described as a federal minimum.

### Conventional financing

Conventional mortgages are not insured or guaranteed under a government mortgage program such as FHA, VA, or USDA. They can be conforming or nonconforming. Conforming financing must satisfy applicable Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac requirements, including the relevant loan limit; being below that limit alone does not establish eligibility. A loan above the applicable conforming limit is commonly called jumbo. Other loans may be nonconforming for reasons besides size. [S1, S2]

Neither “portfolio” nor “nonconforming” means that consumer protection requirements disappear. A portfolio lender's decision to retain a loan does not itself determine its legal classification. Likewise, conforming status and Qualified Mortgage status answer different questions; do not treat the labels as synonyms.

Loan limits depend on the applicable year, location, and number of units. Use FHFA's current county resources rather than a national number copied from an older consumer summary. Ask whether mortgage insurance applies to the proposed conventional loan and how its cost is reflected. Do not promise that every conventional loan requires a large down payment or that every borrower can cancel insurance on demand. [S2, S3]

### FHA insured financing

FHA is part of HUD and provides mortgage insurance on loans made by FHA approved lenders. That insurance protects the lender against covered loss; it does not mean the government has approved a particular consumer's application or will make the consumer's monthly payments. The mortgage must meet applicable insurance requirements. Borrowers pay mortgage insurance premiums through lenders. [S4]

For an actual comparison, verify the proposed FHA transaction's current borrower, property, documentation, financing, and mortgage insurance requirements. Do not assume every FHA loan has identical costs or that FHA is exclusively a first time buyer program. The current Handbook 4000.1 index is the starting point for policy verification, but a newly published handbook can contain provisions with later effective dates. Check the provision that governs the actual transaction. [S5]

A useful borrower explanation is: “FHA insurance may make this financing option available through an approved lender. We still need to evaluate your application and property under the applicable requirements, and include mortgage insurance in the cost comparison.” This explains the benefit without describing insurance as guaranteed approval.

### VA backed financing

A VA Certificate of Eligibility, or COE, documents eligibility for the home loan benefit. A VA backed purchase loan also requires satisfaction of VA and lender credit, income, and other requirements, along with the applicable occupancy requirement. A COE alone does not approve the mortgage. VA backed purchase financing does not require PMI or FHA MIP. A one time funding fee may apply, with exemptions for qualifying borrowers. Other closing costs can still exist. [S6, S7]

Avoid the shortcut “VA means no cash needed.” A no down payment possibility does not erase closing costs, price and appraisal issues, entitlement questions, or lender review. Determine which benefits and restrictions apply to this borrower and proposed transaction. Funding fee exemption, if relevant, is a fact to verify rather than a status to assume from appearance or an informal statement.

### USDA guaranteed financing

The USDA Section 502 Guaranteed Loan Program works through approved lenders for eligible households purchasing or otherwise financing qualifying primary residences in eligible rural areas. Property location and household income eligibility matter. An address that looks rural is not sufficient evidence; use USDA's official eligibility resources and the applicable review process. Household income eligibility is distinct from deciding what income can support repayment. [S8, S29]

USDA also has a separate direct loan program. Do not interchange the direct and guaranteed programs' eligibility rules, application channels, or terms. Guaranteed financing may offer no down payment for qualifying borrowers, but that does not make the transaction cost free or remove credit and repayment review. Program guarantees reduce a lender's risk; they do not excuse the borrower's repayment obligation. [S8, S9]

### Compare the same transaction

Gather written terms for the same purpose, property, loan amount, term, and rate structure wherever possible. If a difference is intentional, explain it. Compare principal and interest, mortgage insurance or applicable program fees, estimated taxes and insurance, cash needed at closing, remaining borrower resources, and features that change later. State which amounts are estimates and which assumptions could change. Total monthly payment can differ from principal and interest alone. [S3, S10]

A low initial payment might reflect a smaller loan, financed costs, a temporary feature, or expenses omitted from the quote. Investigate the cause before calling one option better. A larger loan caused by financed charges is still debt. A permitted gift or assistance source also needs its actual terms reviewed; an obligation with deferred repayment is not automatically a grant.

### Worked example 4A Comparing a cash and payment tradeoff

Fictional borrower Mira receives two illustrative quotes for the same $285,000, 30 year fixed rate loan. The comparison assumes identical nonloan expenses and no financed fees. Offer Alder requires $8,400 of net upfront loan costs and a $1,925 monthly principal and interest payment. Offer Birch requires $6,400 of net upfront loan costs and a $1,975 monthly principal and interest payment. These are supplied exercise figures, not market quotes or program minimums.

Birch saves $2,000 initially but costs $50 more in each stipulated monthly payment. Dividing $2,000 by $50 gives 40 monthly payments. This is a simplified nominal payment difference comparison, not a full economic break even analysis. It omits time value, tax effects, the balance remaining when the loan ends, and costs not stipulated equal. It cannot establish suitability.

If Mira expects to keep the loan for only 18 months, the stipulated payment difference is $900; at 60 months it is $3,000. Those calculations help frame questions about liquidity and holding period. They do not authorize predicting a refinance, disregarding other costs, or selecting a program before eligibility is reviewed.

### Learner case 4A Eligibility evidence

Fictional borrowers Alex and Nia want a principal residence and are considering two properties. Alex has a COE. One property is described by its seller as “USDA eligible,” but no address check or household income evaluation has been completed. Their loan officer says, “Choose either government program and your approval is assured.”

In four short bullets, identify the unsupported promise, one VA verification still needed, two USDA eligibility facts to establish, and one cost comparison that remains useful. Then write one sentence replacing the promise without discouraging either option prematurely. Do not invent a credit score, debt ratio, fee, or loan limit.

### Optional self-review 4A Explaining the guarantee

Write a two or three sentence answer to the fictional borrower question: “If the government guarantees it, why do you still need my documents?” Explain whose risk the protection addresses and why verification remains necessary. Add why no down payment does not necessarily mean no cash to close. Check your wording for an unsupported approval promise, then revise it using the lesson. An under one minute spoken explanation or a discussion with someone you choose offline is optional. No peer or instructor response is provided by this practice.

## Unit 4B Processing and closing

Proposed future OIL allocation, 50 minutes: instruction and worked example 20; applied practice 20; peer and instructor dialogue with revision 5; formative checks and feedback 5.

### From information to an authorized decision

Processing organizes and verifies the information needed for the lending decision. Underwriting evaluates the borrower, property, and proposed financing against applicable requirements. Requests for additional evidence can arise because a document is incomplete, a fact has changed, or the existing information does not resolve a condition. Sending a document is not the same as having the condition accepted. [S11, S12]

Track the actual stage: requested, received, reviewed, accepted, or still unresolved. These are practical workflow descriptions rather than mandatory federal software labels. For each unresolved item, identify the issue, responsible person, evidence needed, and next follow up. A useful record might say, “Updated statement received; source of recent deposit remains under review.” “Bank statement done” hides the remaining question.

Prequalification and preapproval are not universally standardized promises. Lenders use these terms differently, and letters may contain conditions or expiration dates. Read what was evaluated and what the letter actually commits to. Do not describe a preliminary letter as a guaranteed loan offer merely because its title sounds strong. [S13]

### The people have different responsibilities

The loan officer explains options and coordinates the application. Processing staff assemble and verify supporting material. The lender's underwriting function evaluates credit and property information and makes the applicable decision through its authorized process. An automated recommendation does not justify ignoring inaccurate inputs, required documentation, or outstanding conditions. [S11, S12]

Title and settlement work addresses ownership, title matters, documents, funds, and the closing under the applicable local structure. The person conducting closing may be a settlement agent, escrow agent, or attorney. Practices and legal requirements vary by state. Title work and credit underwriting are related but separate: a title issue can block an otherwise acceptable credit file, and a clean title report cannot approve the borrower's income. [S14, S15]

A coordinator should not promise a legal title conclusion or instruct someone to ignore a recorded lien. Route title and lien questions to the designated title professional or counsel, and credit conditions to underwriting. Make the handoff concrete by stating what document or fact needs review. This is more useful than sending an unexplained message marked “urgent.”

### Closing readiness has several parts

Before representing a file as ready, distinguish underwriting conditions, disclosure requirements, settlement conditions, and authorization to disburse. A scheduled appointment does not prove these are satisfied. Signing, consummation, funding, recording, and possession can be separate events. Which event creates a legal obligation or permits a particular release depends on applicable law and transaction facts.

For transactions subject to the Loan Estimate and Closing Disclosure rules, compare the latest accurate documents and resolve unexplained changes. The Closing Disclosure generally must be received at least three business days before consummation; coverage, counting, corrections, and exceptions belong to Module 5. The instruction here is to flag timing questions to the designated compliance reviewer, not to announce that a calendar date or every fee revision automatically restarts a waiting period. [S16]

Certain credit transactions secured by a consumer's principal dwelling have a federal right of rescission. A purchase money residential mortgage transaction is generally exempt. Not every refinance is rescindable: the same creditor exception and new advance rules, among other coverage details, matter. A second home is not automatically a principal dwelling. Do not promise same day refinance disbursement or a cancellation right merely from the word “refinance.” Route the actual transaction for the Module 5 analysis. [S17]

### Closing costs and cash to close answer different questions

Closing costs are charges associated with obtaining the mortgage and completing the transaction. Cash to Close is the amount the consumer must bring to closing, or in applicable transactions receive, after the relevant loan proceeds, deposits, credits, payoffs, and adjustments are accounted for. The down payment is not itself a closing cost. Money already deposited should not be collected again without the correct reconciliation. [S18]

Loan related charges, prepaids, and initial escrow deposits also serve different purposes. Prepaid interest covers the applicable initial interest period. An initial escrow deposit establishes funds to pay identified future bills. Calling an escrow deposit a lender fee obscures its purpose. Conversely, an initial deposit does not guarantee that future taxes or insurance costs will stay unchanged. [S18]

Use a sources and uses worksheet to test completeness, then reconcile it to the actual disclosures and settlement documents. Do not assume a seller credit can pay every category, exceed program limits, or become unrestricted cash back. Verify the credit's agreed amount, permissible use, and correct placement. If a disclosed total already includes a lender credit, subtracting that credit again produces a false result.

### Worked example 4B Reconciling the remaining contribution

Fictional borrower Luca purchases a home for $360,000 using a $324,000 loan. Gross borrower closing charges before credits are $10,800. This exercise expressly includes all relevant loan charges, prepaids, and initial escrow funding. A $9,000 earnest money deposit is already paid and credited. A $3,600 seller credit and $1,200 lender credit are stipulated permissible, approved, and fully usable. There are no other prorations, payoffs, financed charges, or adjustments.

The difference between price and loan is $36,000. Add $10,800 of gross closing charges to obtain $46,800. Subtract the $9,000 deposit and $4,800 total credits. Remaining cash to close is $33,000.

Check the other side: price plus gross charges is $370,800. Sources are the $324,000 loan, $9,000 deposit, $33,000 remaining borrower contribution, and $4,800 credits, totaling $370,800. The figures balance. That establishes the exercise arithmetic; it does not establish actual underwriting approval, lawful credit use, or permission to release funds.

Suppose the lender credit falls to $700, with every other stipulated fact unchanged. The remaining contribution increases by $500 to $33,500. The coordinator should reconcile the changed terms with the creditor and settlement team and route any disclosure consequences for review. Do not tell Luca the amount is unchanged because “closing costs were already approved.”

### Protect the handoff of funds

Borrowers should confirm the form of acceptable closing payment with the closing agent. “Cash to close” usually means a verified transfer or cashier's check rather than currency brought to the table. Verify wire instructions through an independently established trusted contact channel, especially when an unexpected message changes the account. A familiar name in an email is not verification. [S11, S19]

Provide an accurate status update when a condition remains. “The credit decision is conditional on the updated evidence, and settlement has a separate title question” is informative. “Everything is approved; sign now and we will fix it later” creates an expectation that the known facts do not support.

### Learner case 4B Two unresolved decisions

Fictional borrower Elena has a conditional approval for a $250,000 loan. The underwriter still needs acceptable evidence explaining a recent deposit. The settlement agent also reports an unreleased prior lien. Elena's closing appointment is tomorrow. An assistant has marked both items complete because the borrower emailed a bank statement and said the old lien was paid.

Prepare a five line status note: describe each unresolved issue, name its decision owner, identify why the received information is not itself acceptance, and state what cannot yet be promised. Add a one sentence response to an email changing the wire destination and asking for immediate payment. Do not decide the title question or compute a disclosure deadline from incomplete facts.

### Optional self-review 4B Answering a closing question

In two or three sentences, answer the fictional question, “My costs are $10,800, so why am I bringing $33,000?” Use Luca's figures to explain the down payment, deposit, and credits. Check that each amount is counted once. Explain why a balanced worksheet does not guarantee funding, and revise any wording that confuses arithmetic with condition clearance. Keep the response for your own review or discuss it offline if you choose; instructor feedback and peer participation are not supplied here.

## Unit 4C Servicing after closing

Proposed future OIL allocation, 50 minutes: instruction and worked example 25; applied practice 10; peer and instructor dialogue with revision 10; formative checks and feedback 5.

### Find the right company and the right record

The originator helps arrange the mortgage. The owner holds the loan interest. The servicer administers the account, including payments and applicable escrow activity. These roles can be held by different organizations. A borrower may reasonably return to the original loan officer with a servicing question, but that does not give the officer authority to alter the account. [S30, S31]

Start with the statement, transfer notice, escrow analysis, or payoff quote relevant to the question. Identify the claimed discrepancy and its dates. Keep payment receipts and correspondence. Do not tell a borrower a balance is wrong simply because it differs from a number remembered at origination. Equally, do not dismiss a mismatch without identifying its components.

### A servicing transfer does not suspend payment duties

For covered loans, servicing transfer notices identify the effective date, the new servicer, and when payments move. Regulation X generally requires notice by the old servicer at least 15 days before transfer and by the new servicer within 15 days afterward, subject to specified exceptions and combined notice rules. The transfer itself does not alter mortgage terms other than terms directly related to servicing. [S21]

The important payment protection is precise. During the 60 days beginning on the effective transfer date, a payment the old servicer receives by the applicable due date, including any contractual grace period, cannot be treated as late for any purpose. This protects a timely payment sent to the wrong servicer. It is not a 60 day payment holiday, and mailing late is not made timely merely because transfer occurred. [S21]

Follow the verified notice for future payments, check automatic payment arrangements, and examine subsequent statements. If an otherwise protected payment is marked late, preserve proof of receipt and route the error through the servicer's designated process. Avoid promising how quickly a credit record will change or assuming autopay transferred automatically. [S20]

### Fixed rate does not freeze every housing expense

A standard fully amortizing fixed rate loan can have unchanged scheduled principal and interest while its total payment changes. Escrow generally collects money for expenses such as property taxes and homeowners insurance. Different tax bills, insurance premiums, or permitted adjustments after account analysis can change the required escrow collection. Costs paid separately, such as some association charges, remain part of the household budget even though they are absent from the mortgage payment. [S10]

A shortage means the balance is below the required target; a deficiency means the account is negative. These are different account conditions. Escrow rules govern analysis, collection, statements, and the treatment of surpluses or shortages. Do not prescribe an arbitrary cushion, promise an automatic refund, or say every borrower can demand an escrow waiver. Actual account facts, applicable law, program requirements, and the agreement matter. [S22]

### Worked example 4C Explaining a changed payment

Fictional borrower Rowan's scheduled principal and interest is $1,700 monthly. The prior escrow collection was $400, making the stipulated payment $2,100. The new account analysis identifies $450 monthly for ongoing taxes and insurance and an allowed $600 shortage repayment spread over 12 months. Assume the analysis and repayment arrangement have been independently verified for this exercise; no mortgage insurance or other payment component applies.

Shortage recovery is $600 divided by 12, or $50 monthly. The new payment is $1,700 plus $450 plus $50, totaling $2,200. The $100 increase has two parts: $50 for higher ongoing escrow needs and $50 for shortage recovery. None of these figures indicates a changed note rate.

After the stipulated shortage is repaid, do not guarantee that the total becomes $2,150 forever. That would require ongoing escrow needs to remain $450 and no other adjustment to apply. Explain the current analysis, identify the temporary component, and direct questions about projected bills to the servicer. This exercise is arithmetic using supplied facts, not a rule prescribing every shortage repayment schedule.

### Payoff requires a date and a reliable quote

A statement balance is not necessarily the amount needed to satisfy the loan on a future date. A payoff includes applicable interest through the intended payoff date and can include other unpaid amounts. A permitted prepayment charge, if applicable, also matters. Request the current payoff from the lender or servicer, identify its good through date and instructions, and reconcile it with the contemplated closing. [S23]

For example, if a fictional statement shows $180,000 principal and the verified payoff supplies $420 accrued interest plus $80 of applicable unpaid charges, the stipulated payoff is $180,500. Do not substitute the principal figure or assume a remembered escrow balance can be netted against it. If payment will arrive later than the quoted date, obtain the appropriate updated amount or verified per diem instruction. Satisfaction of the debt and the required release of its lien must both be handled through the proper process; recording requirements vary by state.

### Respond early to payment difficulty

A borrower who expects to miss a payment should contact the servicer promptly and can seek a HUD approved housing counselor. Loss mitigation can involve different arrangements depending on the account and available programs. A forbearance may pause or reduce payments temporarily, but does not itself forgive the missed amount. A modification changes loan terms through an approved arrangement; it should not be promised before evaluation. [S24, S25]

Federal servicing protections have coverage rules and exceptions. Regulation X does not require a servicer to offer a particular loss mitigation option merely because a borrower requests it. Foreclosure rights and procedures also depend on applicable state law. An originator should recognize urgency, provide verified contact channels, and route legal questions rather than predict a sale date or tell the borrower that a submitted application automatically stops every proceeding. [S26, S27]

Be alert to a person demanding upfront fees, guaranteed relief, title transfer, or payments redirected away from the verified servicer. Preserve the message and help the borrower identify legitimate assistance. Never recommend intentionally missing payments as a shortcut to approval. [S28]

### Learner case 4C Transfer confusion

Fictional borrower Sam's covered loan transfers servicing on October 1. The payment is due October 1 and the contract allows a grace period through October 15. The old servicer receives the full payment October 8. The new statement shows a late fee for that payment. Sam also expects difficulty paying November's installment and says, “The transfer gives me two months off anyway.”

Give four short responses: explain the October payment protection using the supplied receipt date, correct the proposed payment holiday, identify evidence and the appropriate servicing contact, and explain the next step for the separate November hardship. Do not promise a modification or treat an unverified phone statement as a changed payment agreement.

### Optional self-review 4C Explaining the next step

In two or three sentences, answer the fictional question, “My rate is fixed, and you said my payment was $2,100. Why is it $2,200?” Separate Rowan's unchanged principal and interest from ongoing escrow and shortage recovery. Identify the record needed before asserting an error, and check that your response does not promise a permanent future payment. Revise against the lesson and public process criteria. An offline discussion is optional; this self-review does not provide or replace the genuine exchanges required by the proposed future OIL design.

## Working glossary

Conventional mortgage: a mortgage outside government insurance or guaranty programs. Conforming mortgage: financing meeting applicable enterprise purchase requirements. COE: VA evidence of eligibility for the home loan benefit. Underwriting: evaluation of borrower, collateral, and transaction eligibility. Condition: an unresolved requirement attached to a decision or closing step. Settlement agent: the professional coordinating the closing within the applicable local structure. Cash to close: the reconciled amount due from or to the consumer at closing. Escrow analysis: review of account funding and projected disbursements. Servicer: the company administering the mortgage account. Payoff: the amount necessary to satisfy the debt as of a specified date. Forbearance: an agreed temporary payment pause or reduction with repayment obligations remaining. Loss mitigation: processes and options intended to address delinquency and potential foreclosure.

## Unit 5A TILA and the disclosure timeline

Proposed future OIL allocation, 45 minutes: instruction 20; legal case 13; peer/instructor dialogue and revision 8; formative checks 4.

### Start with coverage

The Truth in Lending Act is implemented principally through Regulation Z. It promotes informed use of consumer credit and includes substantive mortgage protections as well as disclosure duties. Personal, family or household purpose matters. Calling a loan an investment or having a borrower sign a business-purpose statement does not replace analysis of its actual purpose and the relevant exemptions. [P5-01]

The integrated Loan Estimate (LE) and Closing Disclosure (CD) rules generally cover closed-end consumer credit secured by real property or a cooperative unit. They do not apply to every loan bearing the word mortgage. HELOCs and reverse mortgages have different disclosure frameworks; a loan secured only by a manufactured home that is personal property requires separate analysis. A construction purpose does not automatically exclude a covered real-property loan. The correct question is what this provision covers, not whether another product has a similar name. [P5-02]

RESPA and Regulation X have their own coverage rules for federally related mortgage loans and exclusions. ECOA has broader credit coverage than TILA. A loan outside TRID can still be subject to other federal duties. Use one coverage entry per law rather than one global exempt box. [P5-03, P5-12]

### Interest rate, finance charge and APR

The note rate determines interest under the loan terms. The finance charge expresses credit cost in dollars under a defined inclusion/exclusion test; it is not automatically the sum of every settlement expense. The annual percentage rate expresses the cost of credit as a yearly rate using the legally prescribed method. Certain bona fide and reasonable real-estate-related charges can be excluded from the finance charge under stated conditions. A fee's label alone does not decide inclusion. [P5-04, P5-05]

Suppose two fictional fixed-rate loans have the same principal, note rate, payment schedule and term. One charges more prepaid finance charges. Their note-rate payments may match while their APRs differ. That teaches why rate alone is incomplete. It does not justify adding a percentage of fees to the note rate as a compliant APR calculation. Use a validated calculation and the applicable accuracy rules. For comparisons, also consider cash required, the consumer's expected holding period and risks that an APR does not summarize.

A learner can explain an APR without promising that the lowest APR is always the best individual choice. Likewise, an APR change is not automatically an inaccurate APR. Later CD restart analysis uses the accuracy standard in Regulation Z, not simply whether the displayed digits changed. [P5-05]

### An application can arrive before a completed file

For the covered TRID transaction, six submitted items establish the application: the consumer's name, income, Social Security number to obtain a credit report, property address, estimated property value, and mortgage loan amount sought. If a consumer lacks a Social Security number, the official interpretation permits another unique identifier used to obtain the credit report. Verification documents, a signed purchase contract and underwriting approval are not extra prerequisites. Record when the last of the six arrived, including through an authorized intake channel. Do not replace that event with the date someone created the loan in software. [P5-06]

The initial LE must ordinarily be delivered or mailed no later than the third business day after application. That deadline uses days on which the creditor's offices are open to the public for substantially all business functions. Delivery or mailing must also occur at least seven business days before consummation; that waiting period uses all calendar days except Sundays and the specified legal public holidays. The two definitions cannot be interchanged. A timely denial or withdrawal within the initial period can implicate an exception; it does not erase independent ECOA duties. [P5-02, P5-06]

Before the consumer receives the LE and indicates intent to proceed, fees generally cannot be imposed, except a bona fide and reasonable credit-report fee. Acknowledging receipt does not itself necessarily express intent to proceed. A creditor may ask for documents, but cannot require verification documents before providing the LE. Record intent through a permitted process; do not treat silence as consent. [P5-02]

### Worked calendar: one file, three separate events

Harbor Pine Lending is open for substantially all business functions Monday through Friday. The case dates have no intervening legal public holiday. On Monday, September 14, 2026, it receives all six TRID elements. A processor enters the file on Wednesday 16. Pay stubs arrive Friday 18. The LE is delivered in person Thursday 17. An accurate CD is received in person Tuesday 22. There are no restart events.

The initial LE deadline is Thursday 17: Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday are the three creditor business days after application. Wednesday's software entry does not move the trigger. For the seven-day LE wait beginning with Thursday delivery, count Friday 18, Saturday 19, Monday 21, Tuesday 22, Wednesday 23, Thursday 24, Friday 25. For the CD wait, count Wednesday 23, Thursday 24, Friday 25. On these stipulated facts both waiting periods permit consummation Friday 25, assuming all other requirements are met. Saturday counts in the waiting periods even though the lender is closed. [P5-02, P5-06]

Now replace in-person CD receipt with mailing on Tuesday 22 and no evidence of earlier actual receipt. Presumed receipt is Friday 25. Count Saturday 26, Monday 28, Tuesday 29 for the CD wait. Mailing Tuesday does not permit Friday consummation under those assumptions. Electronic delivery must satisfy applicable E-Sign requirements; an email sent timestamp alone does not establish actual same-day receipt. [P5-02]

### Consummation is not automatically funding

Consummation occurs when the consumer becomes contractually obligated on the credit transaction under applicable state law. Signing, funding, recording and delivery of possession can occur at different times. Establish the legally relevant event rather than moving a disclosure deadline by relabeling the closing. A settlement appointment is a proposed schedule, not evidence that a legal waiting period is complete. [P5-06]

### Rescission is a separate right and clock

Certain consumer transactions secured by a consumer's principal dwelling carry a right to rescind. A residential mortgage transaction used to acquire or initially construct that dwelling is generally exempt from this rescission right. A same-creditor refinancing has a specific exemption with a new-advance qualification. Do not reduce these rules to every refinance has three days or every purchase has a cancellation period. A person whose ownership interest is encumbered may have rescission rights without signing the note. [P5-07]

For an ordinary covered rescindable transaction, the consumer may rescind until midnight of the third business day after the last of consummation, delivery of the required rescission notice, or delivery of the material disclosures. Here business day excludes Sundays and the specified legal public holidays. If all three events occur Friday, September 25, the ordinary period ends midnight Tuesday 29: Saturday is day one, Monday day two, Tuesday day three. This is after consummation, unlike the pre-consummation CD wait. Disbursement ordinarily waits for expiration and the creditor's reasonable satisfaction that the consumer has not rescinded. Defects and exceptions require review; the example is not a funding authorization. [P5-07]

### Your timeline case

For a new file, all six items arrive Monday, September 21, 2026. The lender's business schedule is Monday-Friday. There are no relevant holidays. The LE is delivered in person Thursday 24. The CD is received in person Monday 28. No exception, waiver or restart event applies.

Keep delivery, presumed receipt and consummation in separate rows. For optional self-review, show the count and the definition used for each row rather than recording a date alone.

## Unit 5B Settlement charges, revisions and referrals

Proposed future OIL allocation, 40 minutes: instruction 18; legal case 10; peer/instructor dialogue and revision 8; formative checks 4.

### Follow the service and the money

RESPA section 8 and Regulation X prohibit giving or accepting a thing of value under an agreement or understanding for referrals of covered settlement-service business. They separately prohibit splitting a settlement charge other than for services actually performed. An agreement can be inferred from conduct; a referral arrangement need not be written. A gift, paid marketing expense or discounted service can carry value. Disclosing a prohibited referral payment does not make it lawful. [P5-08]

Payments for actual services and other specified permitted arrangements require their own conditions. Calling a payment advertising does not establish that the service exists or that compensation reflects reasonable market value. The value of referrals cannot be built into the valuation. An affiliated-business arrangement requires analysis of disclosure, required use and permitted returns; a common owner is neither an automatic ban nor an automatic exemption. [P5-08, P5-09]

Worked example: a title firm offers an unrelated mortgage lender's originator $90 for every covered loan referred to it. The originator is not the title firm's employee; there is no separate service or applicable exception. A borrower disclosure and an invoice labeled outreach do not change what is being bought. The originator should decline and escalate the arrangement through the firm's process. Contrast a proposed fixed-price advertisement with identified deliverables: you still need evidence of actual services, reasonable value and no payment for referrals before concluding that the arrangement is permissible. Do not infer compliance merely because compensation is flat rather than per loan.

### Classify a fee before calculating a tolerance

The LE good-faith comparison starts with the legally usable estimate. Typical categories are:

- General, commonly called zero tolerance: creditor or broker fees, affiliate service fees, required third-party services for which shopping is not permitted, and transfer taxes
- Ten-percent aggregate: recording fees and qualifying required unaffiliated services where shopping is permitted and the consumer selects a provider on the required written list
- Permitted variations: specified prepaid interest, property insurance, escrow and property-tax charges, plus qualifying outside-list selections and services not required by the creditor

These are abbreviated navigation labels, not substitutes for the rule. Paragraph (e)(3)(iii) has specific bona-fide-charge provisions, including for listed charges paid to an affiliate; therefore anything involving an affiliate is always zero tolerance is overbroad. Shopping must be real, and the provider list must meet the rule. A missing list creates a compliance issue but does not always turn an unaffiliated shoppable service into zero tolerance. An estimate without a percentage cap still requires good-faith diligence. [P5-02]

### Worked charge ledger

Assume all three services below are correctly in the ten-percent aggregate, all were performed, amounts are exact dollars, no valid revised baseline exists, and all other requirements are satisfied.

| Charge | Valid estimate | Final consumer charge |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Recording fees | $250 | $265 |
| Required unaffiliated title service, chosen from list | $800 | $920 |
| Required unaffiliated survey, chosen from list | $250 | $245 |
| Total | $1,300 | $1,430 |

The aggregate ceiling is $1,300 multiplied by 1.10, or $1,430. The title line rose 15%, but the applicable aggregate has not exceeded its ceiling. If the title charge instead becomes $960, the final aggregate becomes $1,470 and the excess is $40. Do not refund 10% of every fee, or treat each line as its own ten-percent bucket. Do not add an estimated service that was never performed to create extra cushion. [P5-02]

Now consider a separate zero-tolerance origination fee of $1,200 estimated and $1,260 charged, with no permissible revised baseline. A $60 decrease in an unrelated zero-tolerance fee does not net away this $60 increase. Keep each relevant test separate.

A tolerance comparison also does not prove a settlement charge is permissible. Suppose an appraisal is estimated at $700, the consumer is charged $700, and the provider actually receives $650 for the entire service. No lawful average-charge program or other service exists. The unchanged LE-to-CD number does not justify retaining the extra $50. Regulation Z's actual-charge provision is a distinct test. A genuine average-charge program has specific eligibility, uniformity, calculation and record conditions; it cannot be invented retrospectively for a convenient file. [P5-02]

### A changed fact is not a blanket reset

Permitted revision paths include qualifying changed circumstances affecting charges or eligibility, consumer-requested changes, rate-lock events for rate-dependent terms, and other specified situations. Determine the reason, affected charge and amount, when sufficient information arrived, and applicable timing. A clerical error or an invoice reflecting facts already available is not automatically a changed circumstance. A revision justified for one fee does not reprice every unrelated fee. For an aggregate charge, an event below the applicable aggregate threshold does not automatically reset the comparison baseline. [P5-02]

A revised LE used for the permitted comparison generally must be delivered or mailed within three creditor business days after receiving sufficient information to establish the reason. The consumer must receive it no later than four precise business days before consummation. A revised LE cannot be provided on or after the date the CD is provided. When a permitted event occurs too late for a revised LE, the CD route has its own requirements. These are separate clocks, not one three-day rule. [P5-02]

Worked decision: a lender initially omits its known $75 processing charge, then finds the omission in its own checklist. A colleague proposes issuing a new LE and using the higher amount because the borrower has not objected. The missing fact is not the borrower's objection. It is a legally permitted revision reason linked to that increase. Preserve the error and obtain the authorized correction decision; do not manufacture a changed-circumstance explanation.

### CD correction is not always a new wait

A corrected CD must be handled under the applicable provision. Before consummation, three specified changes require a new three-business-day waiting period: an APR that becomes inaccurate under the relevant accuracy rule, a specified change in loan product, or addition of a prepayment penalty. Other changes generally require corrected disclosure at or before consummation without automatically restarting the wait. A changed fee can affect APR; therefore fee changes never restart is also wrong. [P5-02, P5-05]

If the consumer pays amounts exceeding the permitted good-faith tolerance, Regulation Z provides a refund and corrected-CD process within 60 days after consummation. Do not describe that as a universal deadline for every legal defect or permission to knowingly overcharge at closing. The proper CD also needs supported amounts, payees and payment columns. An accurate subtotal does not cure a placeholder payee or failure to deliver the form to a required consumer. [P5-02, P5-10]

### Your settlement case

A proposed closing has a ten-percent aggregate valid estimate of $900 and final qualifying charges of $1,015. All services were performed; no permitted revision exists. Separately, the lender's own zero-tolerance fee rises from $800 to $845. An appraisal appears unchanged at $610, but the provider receives $585; there is no lawful averaging program or other service. Nothing has yet been collected.

Record the aggregate ceiling and excess, the independent lender-fee increase, and the separate appraisal issue. Explain why the three questions cannot be answered solely by comparing total cash to close. Identify the records and decision maker needed before release. Do not add a guessed remedy for a defect not covered by the facts.

For optional self-review, defend the baseline you used and test whether the source of an increase matters. As a separate hypothetical, consider a genuinely new borrower-requested change affecting one charge: identify the facts and timing evidence you would need before revising that charge, without inventing an amount or assuming a permissible reset. Leave unrelated analyses intact. A supported alternative is welcome; invented facts are not. You may compare your reasoning with the lesson or discuss it offline if you choose; no instructor response is supplied here.

## Unit 5C Fair application handling and notices

Proposed future OIL allocation, 35 minutes: instruction 15; legal case 10; peer/instructor dialogue and revision 7; formative checks 3.

### An application has more than one legal definition

Under Regulation B, an application is a request for credit made in accordance with the creditor's procedures. Actual practices matter. A completed application contains the information the creditor regularly obtains and considers for the decision; the creditor must exercise reasonable diligence to obtain it. This is different from TRID's six-item application. A missing property address can prevent the TRID trigger while an evaluated and declined request raises ECOA notice duties. [P5-12]

An employee who evaluates a consumer's information, decides the creditor will not approve, and communicates that decision cannot avoid the consequence by calling the conversation prequalification. Conversely, a general explanation of potential terms and the application process does not necessarily make every inquiry a denied application. Record what actually happened. [P5-12, P5-13]

### Use the notice that matches the decision

For the ordinary consumer-credit cases here, assume a creditor that received more than 150 applications in the preceding calendar year, and no special exception. A completed application generally requires notification of approval, counteroffer or adverse action within 30 days. Incompleteness involving information the applicant can provide requires timely action/notice or a compliant written incompleteness notice under the rule. That notice identifies the needed information, a reasonable response period and the consequence of not responding. Silence is not an express withdrawal. [P5-13]

If sufficient information supports a denial on actual credit grounds, do not use missing documents as a false reason. Adverse-action reasons must reflect the real principal factors. The notice must contain the required action, creditor, ECOA/enforcement-agency and reasons or right-to-reasons components. Generic references to internal policy are not enough. Use an approved notice process rather than improvising a legal form. [P5-13]

A notice is not a cure for a faulty underlying decision. If a debt was counted twice, ask the authorized reviewer to correct the analysis as well as the communication. Preserve both the original event and correction. Regulation B generally has a 25-month retention rule for the consumer application records addressed here, with different anchors and extended retention in specified circumstances. TRID has separate retention duties; do not use one law's period as a universal destruction instruction. [P5-14, P5-15]

### FCRA adds a different notice and access test

The Fair Credit Reporting Act regulates access to and use of consumer reports. A permissible purpose is required; knowing a consumer or having technical access does not establish one. Follow the firm's authorized consumer-report workflow and any applicable consent requirements. A report obtained for a credit decision is not available for unrelated curiosity or marketing. [P5-16]

When adverse action is based in whole or in part on a consumer report, FCRA notice requirements can apply alongside ECOA. The FCRA information includes the reporting agency's contact information, its lack of responsibility for the credit decision, and the consumer's rights to obtain a free report within 60 days and dispute accuracy. When a credit score is used, additional score disclosures apply. The reporting agency's score factors are not necessarily the creditor's actual ECOA denial reasons. A properly designed combined notice can address both laws, but simply sending a score does not do so. [P5-16, P5-17]

Risk-based pricing and mortgage credit-score disclosures have separate rules and exceptions. Approval at a less favorable price does not mean no consumer-report disclosure can be required. Identify the transaction and current rule rather than treating the adverse-action form as the only FCRA document. [P5-17, P5-18]

### Equal treatment and the purpose of monitoring

ECOA prohibits discrimination on specified bases, including race, color, religion, national origin, sex, marital status, age when the applicant can contract, receipt of public-assistance income, and good-faith exercise of rights under the Consumer Credit Protection Act. Evaluate permissible evidence consistently. Reg B's current discouragement provision addresses statements directed at applicants or prospective applicants that the creditor knows or should know would cause a reasonable person to believe credit would be denied or offered on less favorable terms because of a prohibited characteristic. [P5-19]

The Fair Housing Act separately prohibits discrimination in covered residential real-estate-related transactions based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status or disability. The lists and scopes are not identical. Do not assume a state's additional protections disappear because they are absent from a federal list. PE06 practices these ethical and fair-treatment decisions in greater depth. [P5-20]

HMDA and Regulation C require covered institutions to collect, report and disclose specified mortgage information for public-policy purposes, including identifying possible discriminatory lending patterns. HMDA is not a loan-approval standard. Coverage, transaction exclusions and data instructions require current checks. Required demographic collection is not permission to price or deny on a prohibited basis. Preserve the difference between a consumer's response and a permitted observation-based entry under the applicable instructions; never fabricate an answer to make a field look complete. [P5-21]

For a covered first-lien dwelling application, Regulation B also requires notice of the right to receive appraisal/valuation copies and timely copies, generally promptly upon completion or three business days before consummation, whichever is earlier, subject to the rule's waiver provisions. A waiver of timing is not a waiver of the copy itself. Denial does not automatically erase the copy obligation. [P5-22]

### Your notice selector

File A: A consumer has asked for financing but has not identified a property. The creditor evaluates the submitted information, decides it will not lend because of documented recent serious delinquency, and communicates the decision. The decision relied in part on a consumer report.

File B: An ordinary application is missing an applicant-provided asset explanation. There is insufficient information for a credit decision. A colleague asks you to mark withdrawn because the consumer has not answered one call.

For each file, identify the application/notice rules to check, the triggering evidence, and the next responsible action. For File A, distinguish the ECOA decision reason from FCRA reporting-agency information. For File B, distinguish a proper incompleteness path from invented withdrawal. You are selecting and routing a notice process, not composing a legally sufficient notice for a real consumer.

For optional self-review, test the claim that no address means no application of any kind. Use one fact and one source to explain your conclusion. Consider separately whether changing the employee's response to a general explanation changes the result, and identify the evidence needed to support that distinction. Save a revised explanation for your own review or optional offline discussion; this is not instructor assessment.

## Unit 5D Recognizing specialized rule checks

Proposed future OIL allocation, 30 minutes: instruction 12; legal case 7; peer/instructor dialogue and revision 7; formative checks 4.

### Ability to repay and Qualified Mortgages

For a covered transaction, the creditor must make a reasonable, good-faith ability-to-repay determination. The general rule requires consideration of income/assets, employment if relied upon, the covered-loan payment, simultaneous-loan payments, mortgage-related obligations, other debts/alimony/child support, DTI or residual income, and credit history, with required verification. A large down payment or likely future refinance is not a substitute. [P5-23]

Qualified Mortgage categories provide specified routes to a presumption of compliance, with different conditions and protections. General QM is not synonymous with conventional, conforming or a universal 43% DTI ceiling. A non-QM loan is not automatically illegal or exempt from applicable ATR duties. Conversely, a product label does not prove the legal conditions were met. Use the current category, pricing, points-and-fees and underwriting requirements and applicable effective dates. [P5-23]

Worked screen: a fictional consumer can afford only an introductory payment. The originator says rising home value will allow refinancing before the increase. Record the future-payment issue and request the required repayment analysis. Do not solve a verification gap by obtaining a statement that the consumer accepts the risk. Disclosure and repayment analysis are distinct obligations.

### HOEPA and HPML are different screens

HOEPA high-cost coverage can arise from APR, points-and-fees or prepayment-penalty tests for covered principal-dwelling credit. It brings additional disclosures, counseling and substantive restrictions. HPML status uses a different APR-to-average-prime-offer-rate comparison for covered principal-dwelling closed-end credit and can bring escrow and appraisal requirements, each with its own exceptions. A loan can need one analysis without satisfying the other's definition. [P5-24, P5-25, P5-26]

For HPML classification, the current basic spreads are at least 1.5 percentage points for a qualifying nonjumbo first lien, 2.5 for a jumbo first lien under the specified Freddie Mac-limit test, and 3.5 for a subordinate lien. Use comparable-transaction APOR in effect when the rate is set, correct lien/loan facts, and the scope of the requirement being tested. Escrow and appraisal provisions contain additional rules; passing one exemption does not exempt every duty. [P5-25]

Example: stipulated covered nonjumbo first lien, applicable APOR 6.00%, APR 7.60%. The spread is 1.60 percentage points, so the stated basic HPML definition is met. That alone neither establishes HOEPA status nor tells you whether every escrow/appraisal requirement applies. These rates are fictional, not current market data. Annual dollar thresholds and points-and-fees tiers should be refreshed for the applicable year, not memorized from this example. [P5-24, P5-25]

### Compensation and advertisements

For covered loan-originator compensation, Regulation Z restricts compensation based on transaction terms or their proxies and addresses dual compensation and steering. A lender-paid label does not remove the rule. The fact that a borrower signs a disclosure does not authorize prohibited compensation. A proposal that pays more for placing a consumer in a costlier product requires review before it is offered or paid. Specific exceptions and permissible structures must be analyzed rather than generalized. [P5-27]

Regulation Z advertising rules require actually available terms, appropriate rate/APR treatment and additional disclosures when stated trigger terms are used. Advertising a particular payment or down payment can trigger repayment disclosures. A teaser payment must not conceal the later obligation or omit required context. A social-media post is not outside the rules merely because it is short. PE06 includes an honest-payment-message exercise; compliance review still must check the actual advertisement and applicable format. [P5-28]

### Privacy, security and suspicious activity

GLBA privacy duties and Regulation P address notices and sharing of nonpublic personal information, including applicable opt-out rights and exceptions. There is no general rule that borrower information may be shared freely once an application exists. Conversely, not every necessary service-provider disclosure requires the same opt-out process. Identify the recipient, information, purpose and applicable provision. Security safeguards are a separate obligation; a privacy notice does not secure an inbox. [P5-29, P5-30]

For financial institutions under its jurisdiction, the FTC Safeguards Rule requires an appropriate information-security program. Mortgage lenders and brokers can be covered. An employee should use approved channels, limit access, verify recipients and escalate an incident promptly under the firm's plan. The firm's compliance/security team must evaluate regulator and consumer notices; a learner should not invent a universal breach deadline or suppress an incident because no loss is yet proven. [P5-30]

FinCEN's rules require covered nonbank residential mortgage lenders and originators to maintain AML programs and make required suspicious-activity reports. Program elements include risk-based controls, a compliance officer, ongoing training and independent testing. A discrepancy is a reason to gather facts and escalate, not automatically proof of crime. Under the applicable SAR rule, reportability includes thresholds and suspicious-transaction conditions; the designated team evaluates them. SARs and information revealing their existence are confidential subject to specified exceptions. Do not alert a borrower that a SAR was filed or promise that one will not be filed. [P5-31, P5-32]

### Your rule-navigation case

A processor flags three issues on a fictional file: the proposed originator payment increases with the interest rate; a salesperson advertises a temporary payment as the permanent payment; and a bank-statement account number differs from the previously verified record. The consumer has not been accused of wrongdoing.

Create three short rows: relevant rule family, evidence still needed, and responsible reviewer. Keep compensation, advertising and identity/security issues separate. Explain why sending a general disclosure does not clear all three. For optional self-review, test one proposed action for unnecessary disclosure of private data. Revise any response that exposes documents in a discussion forum or announces suspected crime as established fact. Use only fictional facts and public process criteria; no instructor review or peer participation is supplied by this practice.

## Practical glossary

- Application trigger: the event satisfying the particular provision's application definition
- APR: credit cost expressed as a yearly rate under the prescribed calculation, distinct from note rate
- APOR: a benchmark derived from low-risk mortgage pricing; the applicable comparison depends on the rule
- Consummation: when the consumer becomes contractually obligated on the credit transaction under applicable law
- Good faith estimate: an estimate subject to the applicable disclosure, diligence, variation and revision rules
- Adverse action: a covered unfavorable credit action as defined by the applicable law, not simply any disappointing conversation
- QM, HPML and HOEPA: separate legal classifications; none is established by a marketing label
- SAR: suspicious activity report; confidential reporting rules do not replace factual internal escalation

## Unit 6A Apply consistent standards to individual facts

### Begin with the decision you control

A new originator may think ethics belongs only to the underwriter who approves or denies a loan. In practice, the originator decides what to explain, which questions to ask, whether to record an applicant's request, and what information to pass to others. A customer can lose a meaningful opportunity before an underwriter sees the file. A helpful tone does not repair an unsupported restriction hidden inside a friendly conversation.

Separate three kinds of guidance. A **legal rule** has an identified scope and authority. A **program or lender requirement** applies when that program or lender actually requires it and must itself be lawful. A **recommended procedure** is a way to perform the work reliably. For example, this module recommends a comparison note that identifies the relevant difference between two files. No cited federal rule requires a worksheet with that exact name. Conversely, a manager cannot waive a legal prohibition by approving an internal exception.

Ask four questions before imposing a different requirement: What specifically differs? Why is that difference relevant to this decision? Which applicable requirement supports the response? Would we respond the same way to another applicant with that fact? The questions organize your work; they do not themselves supply legal clearance. An answer such as “investor preference” needs an identifiable requirement rather than an assumption attached to a familiar label.

### Understand the overlapping protections

Regulation B implements the Equal Credit Opportunity Act. Its prohibited bases include race, color, religion, national origin, sex, marital status, age when the applicant has capacity to contract, public assistance income, and good faith exercise of rights under the Consumer Credit Protection Act. Its definitions also address associations with other people. Certain regular referral and creditor selection activities fall within the creditor definition for the general discrimination and discouragement rules. [P6-01]

The general discrimination rule reaches any aspect of a credit transaction. Its interpretation includes unequal product explanations, additional documentation, and differently applied exceptions for similarly situated applicants. A final approval does not erase earlier prohibited treatment. A stated neutral reason can also be a pretext rather than the actual reason. [P6-02]

The Fair Housing Act separately covers residential real estate related lending. HUD identifies race, color, national origin, religion, sex, familial status, and disability as protected bases. Familial status is not simply another term for marital status. The two federal frameworks overlap but are not identical; state and local protections can add requirements. This module does not treat absence from one list as permission to disadvantage a consumer. [P6-03]

**September 2026 source boundary.** The April 22 2026 Regulation B final rule became effective July 21 2026 and changed provisions on discouragement, disparate impact, and special purpose credit programs. Current section 1002.6(a) does not provide an ECOA effects test and its interpretation addresses intentional use of proxies. A statistical difference can warrant investigation; it is not taught here as a completed ECOA violation by itself. Other laws, applicable court orders, and actual facts require separate review. These exercises focus on concrete treatment and documented assumptions. [P6-04, P6-05]

### First contact must not replace evidence with a stereotype

Under the current discouragement provision, the issue includes a directed oral or written statement the creditor knows or should know would lead a reasonable person to expect denial or worse terms because of a prohibited characteristic. Do not substitute an older training slogan for that text. The current interpretation also distinguishes encouraging one group to apply from discouraging people who were not the intended recipients. [P6-02]

Consider a consumer who asks whether the company offers loans with a long repayment term. “We can explain the available terms and review your repayment resources” preserves a meaningful inquiry. “People your age should not bother applying here” substitutes a characteristic for individual facts. The appropriate correction does not promise approval. It gives accurate information and routes any actual eligibility issue to the authorized reviewer.

A small change in facts can change the needed review. If the consumer reports that the income they intend to use will end soon, the timing is relevant. Record the actual report and identify the evidence needed. Do not convert that specific fact into a policy against everyone of the same age or income category. An honest question about an identified payment stream is different from guessing what someone will earn based on appearance.

### Income and family questions need a defined purpose

Regulation B permits consideration of income amount and probable continuance, but prohibits automatic discounting because income is part time, pension, annuity, other retirement income, or connected to a prohibited basis. Evaluation must address the individual's circumstances. That protection does not make every reported amount verified, guarantee future receipt, or require approval. [P6-05]

Before an inquiry that may elicit alimony, child support, or separate maintenance income, provide the required explanation that the applicant need not reveal it if they do not want it considered. Questions about an obligation to pay support serve a different purpose. Questions about intentions to bear or rear children are prohibited; appropriately neutral inquiries about dependents and related financial obligations are distinguished by the rule. [P6-06]

Use this distinction when reviewing a script. “What income would you like considered?” requires the appropriate support income disclosure when applicable. “Are you planning a baby?” is not a substitute for asking about actual repayment resources. If an applicant voluntarily reports a forthcoming income change, preserve what they actually said without adding a prediction about their family or motivation.

An individually qualified applicant generally cannot be required to add a spouse's credit obligation merely because they are married. A signature needed under applicable state law to make collateral available can be a different matter. The instrument, purpose, and necessity must be established. Joint financial information alone does not establish joint application intent. Do not call a spouse a coapplicant after the fact just to satisfy a software field. [P6-07]

### Worked example W6A The extra condition

Fictional applicants Tessa and Grant seek the same product on the same day. Their relevant verified income, debts, credit, loan amount, property type, LTV, and documentation status are stipulated identical. Each applies individually and qualifies individually under the stated lawful criteria. Neither file has a collateral signature issue. Tessa is told to add a spouse because “women usually need someone else on the obligation.” Grant receives the ordinary process without that demand.

The observed difference is the additional personal liability requirement imposed on Tessa. The employee's recorded explanation supplies a prohibited basis for it. There is no unresolved credit distinction in the facts that supports the demand. The appropriate response is to preserve the instruction, stop using the unsupported condition, and route correction and incident review through the authorized compliance process. It is not to add the same unlawful condition to Grant's file in the name of consistency.

Now change one fact: a competent state law review establishes that a nonapplicant owner must sign a security instrument to make their property interest available. That can justify a properly scoped collateral signature. It does not establish that the owner must assume personal liability on the note. Ask what the signature does before deciding that any difference in signatures is discriminatory. [P6-07]

### Your case C6A The Juniper comparison

Lina and Owen request the same fixed rate purchase product. The supplied record stipulates the same pricing day, credit score, supported monthly income of $7,200, debts, LTV, property type, and eligible options. Their documentation is complete. Lina is a woman; Owen is a man. No other relevant difference or special purpose program is supplied.

Owen receives an explanation of two eligible options and the standard checklist. Lina receives only the higher upfront cost option and a request for two extra months of bank statements. The originator writes, “Women with young families will probably stop working; give her the safer choice.” Nothing in Lina's file reports a planned income change. Both files remain under review.

Write a five line decision record: the two treatment differences; the evidence of their basis; the unsupported assumption; the immediate corrective review needed; and one sentence to Lina that acknowledges the actual issue without promising approval. Do not infer how many children Lina has from the employee's remark or invent a regulatory remedy.

For a separate second round, use this supplied changed fact: Lina's statement, unlike Owen's, contains an unexplained transfer whose source is required under the same lawful funds policy. Explain which proportionate inquiry that fact supports and which earlier conduct it does not justify. A different fact can support a different request without making every other difference legitimate.
